offences.quote: Personation is the deliberate submission of work done by another person or technology (e.g. another student, a friend, a relative, a peer, a tutor, or anyone else, including generative AI and translation software) as if it were one’s own.

Personation is the deliberate submission of work done by another person or technology (e.g. another student, a friend, a relative, a peer, a tutor, or anyone else, including generative AI and translation software) as if it were one’s own.
Plagiarism is the copying or use of the work of others, whether intentionally or unintentionally, as if it were your own.
Fabricating (making up) data, quotes, results or any other aspect of your work should be self-evidently wrong and will be treated as fraud.
This covers a range of offences, from significant instances of plagiarism to exam misconduct.
Collusion is any form of collaboration with another person, including another student, that has not been clearly acknowledged or permitted for assessment purposes
Arranging for another person to falsely identify themselves as a student and take an exam on their behalf would be seen as a particularly severe form of personation and cheating.
if you fail to reference or acknowledge your own work (i.e. anything originally done for other purposes) as clearly as the work of others, then this may be treated as a form of plagiarism

liability.quote: Any breach of the rules, whether intentional or unintentional, will be treated very seriously and may result in penalties which affect your degree.
The most serious forms of fraud are deliberate – fabricating or falsifying work, or omitting significant items, while knowing that this misrepresents the work done (or not done).

Where genuine errors or poor practice occur (e.g. sloppy data handling which brings in false data, or disregarding outliers in results due to a lack of understanding of what they might mean), these will usually be seen as part of the learning process – being awarded a lower mark, rather than being penalised.

detection.quote: LSHTM uses the plagiarism detection service Turnitin UK, which is widely used by universities across the country.
Turnitin is just a tool: it does not make any 'decisions' about students or their work.
Staff have considerable expertise in identifying plagiarism, and all markers look out for assessment irregularities and have access to a variety of tools to assist them.

process.quote: Judgement as to whether a specific offence has occurred will only be made following proper investigation of the case under LSHTM’s procedures.
students will be presumed innocent unless the contrary can be established through formal procedures and on the balance of probabilities.

outcomes.quote: a range of penalties may be invoked – e.g. a reduction of the grade, or an outright fail for the piece of work with a requirement to re-submit.

severe offences may result in students having their registration on a programme terminated, or even being excluded from entry to any further LSHTM examinations or future degree/certificate awards from LSHTM.
Any breach of the rules, whether intentional or unintentional, will be treated very seriously and may result in penalties which affect your degree.
It is not unusual for one or two students a year to fail an entire module or even their entire degree programme due to assessment irregularity issues, including for plagiarism.
Cheating will be treated more seriously and result in heavier penalties than other forms of assessment irregularities.

definitions.quote: The term ‘assessment irregularity’ applies to any suspected instance of plagiarism, cheating, fraud, collusion, personation or other non-standard activity identified in connection with assessed work
Plagiarism is the copying or use of the work of others, whether intentionally or unintentionally, as if it were your own.
Collusion is any form of collaboration with another person, including another student, that has not been clearly acknowledged or permitted for assessment purposes

Personation is the deliberate submission of work done by another person or technology (e.g. another student, a friend, a relative, a peer, a tutor, or anyone else, including generative AI and translation software) as if it were one’s own.
Fraud is the submission of any work which may cause others to regard as true that which is not true.
Cheating is a deliberate attempt to deceive in order to gain advantage in an assessed piece of work, including coursework, in-module assessments and examinations.
